newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak cbank moves to increase interbank liquidity.
newsitem.headline: Slovak cbank moves to increase interbank liquidity.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) on Wednesday moved to increase liquidity on the interbank money market, calling for the country's reference banks to resume quoting obligatory volumes.

"We expect the reference banks (the eight largest Slovak market players) to resume following the agreement on obligatory quoted volumes and spreads in July," NBS Open Market Operations Department head, Peter Andresic, told Reuters.

The NBS has sharply reduced market liquidity by ceasing to hold its daily repo operations, often used by banks for liquidity, to fight downward pressure on the Slovak crown over the past month started by short-selling of crowns in mid-May.
The central bank eventually won the battle for currency stability, but the liquidity squeeze has virtually paralyzed trading in crowns.

Under the reference bank agreement, the eight banks are obliged to quote prices on up to 100 million crown funds with a maturity of up to one month, 50 million crowns with a maturity of up to three months, and 25 million crowns with up to six months.
Andresic said he expected higher liquidity to bring livelier trading on the local money market in July, once the reference bank system was back in place.
He added rates on the interbank market should edge higher in the first days of more liquid trading than they were before the attack on the crown.
Banks last quoted BRIBOR on May 21, when overnight funds traded between 21 and 22 percent, one-week funds between 25.2 and 25.70 percent and three-month money at 21 to 22 percent.
"Rates are likely to be higher than they were before banks stopped quoting the Bratislava Interbank Offered Rate (BRIBOR) one month ago," Andresic said.
In early Tuesday trading, interbank rates funds hovered between 16.5 percent and 18 percent for most maturities.
The NBS expects quoted volumes to be smaller and spreads wider when the reference banks agreement will again become valid, Andresic said.
The NBS has started to add crown funds through repo tenders in recent, but the local market is still short of liquidity.
According to NBS figures, the banking sector lacked 8.51 percent of funds needed to meet minimum reserves requirements later this month.
